name: Jamal Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew and mark the shift hazards on a laminated yellow route map. Before a new driver takes the first run, I walk the edge by the loading face with them and make sure the radio channel is clear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What gives you pride in the job, and what makes it difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like helping people learn the road without treating speed as the main measure of a good shift. The pay is high for the work and I have more than six months saved, so I can support union training without taking money from rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that small tools can help with paperwork, but a human still owns the safety call. I still read the yellow route map before taking a truck out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly driving and checking the road, so this mild change does not make me expect a pay cut. I have more than six months saved and many mines nearby, which gives me room to keep my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current rotation and use the approved assistant only to sort routine notices. I would compare every hazard note with the yellow map before I gave it to the next driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job and income in this version. If the tool saves a few minutes without changing the crew's checks, I can leave it in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop trusting one of those notices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it left out a closure from the radio, I would stop the handover and get the control room to check it. I would rather spend ten minutes resolving a bad note than make the next driver guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the union to get involved in testing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our safety representative to review the test with the operators who use the road. If the notices were complete for a month, I would be comfortable letting the assistant sort those routine items.

say: I would let a small tool help, but people own the **safety call**.
I would still read the **yellow route map** before sending a truck.
think: I think my driving job and pay remain **secure** in this mild picture.
I have savings and nearby mines, so I can **keep my routine**.
do: Keep the **current rotation** and sort routine notices with the approved assistant.
Compare each hazard note with the **yellow map** before handover.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own job and income in this version.
S0.quote: I still read the yellow route map before taking a truck out.
fieldNote: Jamal uses an approved assistant for **routine notices**, not safety decisions.
His **strong savings** and local job options make the mild case secure.
The yellow route map is his **practical handover check**.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and sort routine notices
Wait for a month of complete notices before expanding use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software can take the booking, but it cannot take responsibility for the person sent down the road. I would tell the mine to publish whether team-lead hours and pay change when route planning moves to a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving work is less exposed than the office tasks, but planning and checking are part of what I do as a lead. I would be uneasy about losing that allowance, especially if the company expected me to review more routes without paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the system's route summary with my yellow map and radio log for two weeks. If it were accurate, I would learn that feature during a paid shift and ask the union to set a clear rule for who approves a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the truck job still looks steady, though lead tasks could move to software. I would ask other crew leads what happened to their hours before I decided the change was harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on your pay statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the lead allowance, paid handover time and overtime for each month before and after the tool arrives. If any line fell, I would bring the figures to the union meeting instead of arguing from a rumor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the route summary disagreed with a driver who knows that road, what should happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the operator to show the hazard on the ground and compare it with the radio log. The system can suggest a route, but the person who sees a soft edge must be able to stop the truck.

say: I would say software cannot take **responsibility for the road**.
I would ask the mine to publish changes to **lead hours and pay**.
think: I think my driving job is safer than **office tasks**.
I worry my **lead allowance** could go before I have a new duty.
do: Compare the system’s **route summary** with the yellow map and radio log for two weeks.
Learn the feature on paid time and ask the union for **approval rules**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because lead tasks could move while driving remains.
S1.quote: Software can take the booking, but it cannot take responsibility for the person sent down the road.
fieldNote: Jamal distinguishes **route suggestions** from the operator's safety authority.
He measures impact through specific **pay lines** and paid handover time.
He wants union rules before the tool expands to **more crews**.

steps.text: Compare route summaries with the yellow map and radio log
Ask the union to set paid-time rules for route approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives first, and robots for hands-on work come about three years later. I would ask the mine and union to post actual paid training places, not a general promise that workers can adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots expected around 2031, my truck job could disappear within five years even if AGI itself does not drive. My savings give me options, and I would rather train early than wait until several mines are hiring the same displaced crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union to secure paid training in physical equipment inspection and enroll if a place opened. In 2029, after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for inspection work only if the job involved physical checks and the wage was clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace the task that brings in most of my income within five years. I have more than six months saved and many nearby mines, so I still have time to retrain or move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection post is mostly records and planning that AGI can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not treat it as a protected job; full AGI can take those thinking tasks too. I would ask how much of the work is a physical check and how many posts remain after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine cannot name the pay or the number of remaining posts, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current truck role while asking other mines and the union for real figures. I would not leave a high-paying job for an inspection title without knowing whether the work and wage last.

say: I would explain thinking AI comes first and robots follow **three years later**.
I would request **paid training places**, not a vague promise.
think: My truck job could go by **2031**, even if AGI does not drive.
My savings and nearby mines give me **options** to retrain or move.
do: Enroll in paid training for **physical equipment inspection**.
In 2029, apply only for work with physical checks and a **clear wage**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could replace my main income task within five years.
S2.quote: With robots expected around 2031, my truck job could disappear within five years even if AGI itself does not drive.
fieldNote: Jamal sees **robot exposure** as the direct risk to his earnings.
His strong cushion and many nearby mines give him **options, not certainty**.
He separates physical inspection from **thinking tasks** AGI can handle.

steps.text: Ask the union to secure paid equipment-inspection training
Enroll in paid training for physical equipment inspection
Apply for physical inspection vacancies with clear wages in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the company to start paid apprenticeships before the thinking systems change the office work. I would also say the three-year wait for robots does not guarantee a job on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years gives me time to learn inspection while I still earn a truck wage, and there are plenty of mines nearby. I would not count on records or scheduling as a fallback after AGI, and I would check whether the physical job lasts after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship before 2031 and keep my haul-truck qualification current. In 2032, after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if the employer named the pay and expected duration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time and savings to prepare, but I cannot know how many roles remain. I would keep earning while I train rather than give up a strong wage for an uncertain bridge job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you invest more time in this apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two nearby mines whether the certificate qualifies people for physical inspections and how long they expect to hire for them. If the answers were different, I would take that to the union before choosing a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if the inspection job is only a short bridge before robots arrive, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the wage covered my bills and gave me time to apply elsewhere before 2034. If it did not, I would keep my truck role and continue comparing other openings.

say: I would demand paid apprenticeships before **office tasks change**.
I would not promise the robot delay guarantees **future work**.
think: I have eight years to learn while **earning a truck wage**.
I will check whether physical jobs last after **2034**.
do: In 2032, apply only with stated **pay and duration** from the employer.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can prepare, but future hiring is unknown.
S3.quote: I would also say the three-year wait for robots does not guarantee a job on the other side.
fieldNote: Jamal treats eight years as **time to train**, not a promise.
He rejects desk records as a **fallback after full AGI**.
He checks wages and job duration before accepting a **temporary bridge**.

steps.text: Apply for physical inspection work with stated pay in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union to bargain for paid training while the mine still has time to plan. I would also ask for honest numbers on physical jobs, since robots follow the thinking change by about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before robots gives me room to prepare, and my savings and pay make the near term feel secure. I would still check whether maintenance has enough physical work after 2039 before I put years into that trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current work and join the union delegation asking for paid transition courses and job forecasts. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would review the physical vacancies and pay before deciding whether to change mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income and job look steady for years, and I have a strong cushion. I would not treat a long warning as a reason to leave work before a real option appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before moving into another role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the employer to name the wage, the physical duties and how long the job is expected to last. I would also ask the union to verify the terms before I gave up my current shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the job forecast is uncertain in 2037, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay in my current job and ask other mines for updated figures. I would wait to change until a real vacancy and pay package were on paper.

say: I would ask the union to bargain for **paid training**.
I would request honest numbers on **physical jobs**.
think: My savings and pay make the **near term secure**.
I would check maintenance demand after **2039** before retraining.
do: Join the union delegation requesting **paid courses** and job forecasts.
In 2037, review vacancies and pay before **changing mines**.
feel: I feel **calm** because my job and income look steady for years.
S4.quote: I would not treat a long warning as a reason to leave work before a real option appears.
fieldNote: Jamal has time and savings to **prepare without rushing**.
He asks the union for **forecasts** before making an individual move.
Physical maintenance is not assumed to remain after **robot arrival**.

steps.text: Join the union delegation seeking paid courses and job forecasts
Wait for a confirmed vacancy and pay package before changing mines

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots may reach the truck work by about 2031. Paid training, honest job forecasts and a union transition agreement would help me choose another role without giving up worker protections.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want our crew to have a voice before a machine changes a shift or a wage. I am willing to move when I see a real path, but I do not want workers left to negotiate one by one.

headlineQuote: I want our crew to have a voice before a machine changes a shift or a wage.
portrait: Jamal Rossi is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
He earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of savings.
Plenty of nearby mines give him **other options** if the roster changes.
He **uses AI occasionally**, after checking that a tool works for the crew.
He favors **union bargaining** and paid training over rushed individual changes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until about 2031 before robots threaten his truck work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, honest job forecasts and a union transition agreement would help Jamal choose a next role.
